text: [{"rune":"Hagalaz","text":"Beneath the torn ground, deep roots hold where the wind cannot reach. Above them, one tree stands after the storm, with a strip of bark caught in its branches. Hagalaz leaves change visible without saying what must survive. Kuky, what links you to those before and after may be broken, or it may still be standing.\n✦ Could this change leave something intact without being a punishment?"}]

[{"rune":"Hagalaz","text":"Beneath the torn earth, deep roots hold the only tree left standing after the storm. Hagalaz names the change that leaves some things standing and takes others down. Older branches lie beside the young growth that follows them. Kuky, what remains between generations in your family may be shelter, or it may be silence.\n✦ What remains in your life without everything else having to fall?"}]

[{"rune":"Hagalaz","text":"Out of sight beneath your family’s tree, roots hold soil between stones. After the storm, you see one trunk standing, its bark split. Hagalaz names change that leaves some things standing. Kuky, your link to generations before and after may be what still holds, or what no longer holds.\n✦ What remains in your life when change does not take everything?"}]

[{"rune":"Hagalaz","text":"Beneath your feet, the roots remain unseen while the storm-stripped tree stands beside your home. You see one torn branch caught against its trunk where new buds form. Hagalaz names change that breaks some things without destroying everything. Kuky, your link to those before and after you may be damaged or still holding.\n✦ What remains in your life when something else breaks?"}]

[{"rune": "Hagalaz", "text": "Beneath the field, under the broken branches and flattened grass, the roots are still holding. The storm worked above ground, where everything that could be torn was torn. Hagalaz is the hail that falls hard and shows what was never fastened down. Kuky, a house can lose much and still stand, or it can stand and be changed past recognition.\n✦ When the hail stops, what do you find yourself looking at first — what fell, or what did not?"}]

[{"rune": "Hagalaz", "text": "Underground, where no one looks, the roots hold while the hail strips the branches above. Hagalaz is the storm that takes what was never fastened down. What stands afterward was not made strong by the weather, it was already rooted. Kuky, some of what runs between your people may be loosening now, and some of it may hold through whatever comes.\n✦ When the loud things have passed, which of the quiet ones are still there?"}]

[{"rune": "Hagalaz", "text": "Under the field, out of sight, the roots hold while the hail strips the branches bare. Hagalaz is the sudden weather that takes what was loosely held and leaves the rest standing. What stood before you in this house, and what comes after, grows from the same hidden hold. Kuky, this may be loss in the family line, or it may be what outlasts it."}]

✦ What in your household has roots you have never had to see?

[{"rune": "Hagalaz", "text": "Under the soil, where no one watches, the roots hold while the hail strips the branches above. Hagalaz is the storm that takes what was loosely held and leaves what was anchored. In a family, some of that holding is older than you, and some of it has not been planted yet. This may be a house losing what it never truly fastened down, Kuky, or a house finding out how far down it goes."}]

✦ When the hail has passed, what is still standing — and did you know its roots ran that deep?

[{"rune":"Fehu","text":"At the mountain’s edge, the sheep descend, more numerous than in spring, with small hooves stirring dust. Fehu names wealth kept alive through care and exchange. Even a larger flock needs room to graze. In love, what you give may be freely offered, while what you receive may be enough to sustain you.\n✦ What reaches your hands now, and what grows weaker when it stays there?"}]

[{"rune":"Fehu","text":"At the mountain’s edge, sheep reach lower grass, with more small hooves than in spring. Fehu names wealth that grows when it is tended and shared. The flock stays plentiful while its living needs are met. What you give may be warmth, and what you receive may be room to breathe.\n✦ What comes to you can also pass on; what has your care today?"}]

[{"rune":"Fehu","text":"At your gate, mountain grazing becomes a flock larger than in spring. You count the smaller bodies pressing against wool still caught with burrs. Fehu names wealth that grows through care and can be shared. What you give may be care with room to grow, while what you receive may be care kept close.\n✦ What in your keeping gains strength through exchange?"}]

[{"rune":"Fehu","text":"At the mountain’s foot, you see rough grazing turn to pasture beneath the returning sheep. You count more backs than in spring, with burrs caught in their wool. Fehu names wealth you can nourish and share. What you give may be care finding use, and what you receive may be care freely returned.\n✦ What can you tend without counting on a return?"}]

[{"rune": "Fehu", "text": "Where the mountain pasture ends and the home field begins, the sheep come down, and the flock is larger than the one that went up in spring. Fehu is wealth that was never still — it grazed, it wandered, it came back changed. What is counted in love is counted the same way, by what returned and what grew while out of sight. Between you and another there may be more held than was given, or more given than has yet come home."}]

✦ What you keep close keeps growing; what stands untended thins out — which of these is in your hands now?

[{"rune": "Fehu", "text": "At the edge of the hillside the mountain gives way to the home field, and the sheep come down heavier and more numerous than when they went up. Fehu is that count at the gate — worth that grew while it was out of your hands. What was fed through the summer returns in a form you did not set. Something between you may be holding more than it shows, or waiting to be let out to graze."}]
✦ What flows in can flow out again — is there something in your keeping that only grows by being given?

[{"rune": "Fehu", "text": "At the edge of the pen, the mountain ends and the counting begins. The sheep are down, and the flock is bigger than it was in spring. Fehu is wealth that was never still — it was out grazing, and it came back grown. What you hold may be larger than you reckoned, or waiting on someone to open the gate."}]

✦ Fehu keeps nothing safe for you. What stands untended thins out — what in your hands has not moved lately?

[{"rune": "Fehu", "text": "At the fence line the mountain ends and the home field begins, and the sheep cross over in a slow stream. The flock comes down larger than it went up. Fehu is wealth that was alive before anyone counted it. What you give may be more than you notice, and what returns may be plenty, or simply enough."}]

✦ What sits still tends to thin out — is there something in your hands that has not moved in a while?

[{"rune":"Wunjo","text":"At the table’s edge, you sit down, and someone shifts over without breaking the talk. Wunjo names the ease of having a place without having to explain your arrival. Still, a welcome can sit beside the habit of waiting for it to end. Kuky, you may be learning to stay with what is good.\n✦ Can you notice when something falls into place and your grip loosens for a while?"}]

[{"rune":"Wunjo","text":"Your chair scrapes as you sit with them, and the silence turns to talk without anyone asking why you came. Wunjo names the simple good of being welcome without having to account for yourself. Even here, enjoyment can meet the old habit of holding back. Kuky, you may be slower to dismiss what is already good.\n✦ When something falls into place, can you notice the moment before you tighten your grip again?"}]

[{"rune":"Wunjo","text":"At the edge of the table, you move from standing apart to sitting among them, beside a chipped cup. With Wunjo, you belong without explaining your arrival. You face no question, but silence is not the same as ease. Kuky, you may slowly become less occupied with earning a place already offered.\n✦ Can you enjoy what fits without asking it to last?"}]

[{"rune":"Wunjo","text":"At the edge of the table beside an open window, you become one of those seated, and nobody asks why you came. Wunjo names your place among others without an explanation. You can sit there and still keep your reasons ready. Kuky, your slow change may be enjoying the company without defending your presence.\n✦ Can something good be enough for you without becoming a victory?"}]

[{"rune": "Wunjo", "text": "At the table's edge, the stranger becomes the one who sits down, and no one asks why you came. Wunjo is that quiet turn, where something fits and nothing has to be earned. The friction is that you may keep waiting for the question, ready with your reasons. Kuky, slow change may look like sitting without the answer prepared."}]

✦ When something falls into place, how long do you keep holding it as though it might slip?

[{"rune": "Wunjo", "text": "At the edge of the room the noise thins out, and you cross into a table where a place is already set. No one asks what brought you. Wunjo is that plain ease of being counted in without explaining yourself. The friction is staying seated once the question of whether you earned it starts up again, and perhaps, Kuky, something in you is slowly learning to stay anyway.\n✦ What would it take to loosen your grip on something that is already going well?"}]

[{"rune": "Wunjo", "text": "You step in from the cold and the talk does not stop for you, a place is made at the bench. Wunjo is that — being among others without having to explain why you came. The hard part is staying seated when nothing is asked of you. It may be, Kuky, that you are slowly learning to stay.\n✦ When something falls into place, how long do you let it stay there before you reach to adjust it?"}]

Ehwaz holds trust between you and another, with movement that neither side has to force. It can point to progress made together, while leaving room for different paces. Trust here does not mean you never feel strain. It leaves open whether shared movement gives you strength or asks more of you than you can comfortably give.

Ehwaz holds trust within a partnership. It can mean that you and someone supporting you make progress together without either setting the pace for both. It also leaves room for a harder possibility: keeping pace with someone else may cost you more than the support gives back. The rune does not decide which is true for you.

In this reading, Ehwaz concerns the trust between you and someone you rely on. Its senses of partnership and movement bring attention to how you make progress together. Trust does not require you to move at the same pace in every moment. You may receive support without having to match another person’s effort or expectations. The distinction here is between relying on someone and feeling obliged to keep up with them.

Ehwaz names trust between you and another, where neither carries all the effort or sets every condition. Its sense of partnership includes movement and progress, but does not promise either. In this reading, you have room to consider the difference between relying on someone and having to match their pace. Support may ease your effort, while the terms of that support may add demands.

Ehwaz is the rune of two moving as one. Its sense here is trust — not belief held in the mind, but something worked out between you and whatever carries you, in how you keep step. It holds partnership, motion, steady progress. What it does not hold is solitary effort or speed won by force.

So in your wellbeing, it marks the quality of the arrangement itself: whether the pace is shared, or set by one and matched by the other. Which of those you are living, the rune does not say.

Ehwaz is the rune of two moving as one. Its older sense is the horse and rider, but what it names is partnership — the working arrangement between you and whatever carries you, or whatever you carry.

Here it carries trust. Not trust as feeling, but trust as a practical thing: how much weight one can put on another without either going over.

So the rune holds both sides. Being supported can lighten the effort, and matching someone else's pace can cost you. Which of those is at work, Ehwaz does not say.

Ehwaz is the rune of two moving together. It holds trust, partnership, and progress that depends on more than one party — nothing in it moves alone. The trust it names is practical rather than sentimental: an arrangement that works because each side keeps to its own pace and neither forces the other.

In the matter you brought, that can go either way. Being carried eases the effort. Matching another's speed costs something. Ehwaz names the arrangement; it does not say which weight falls to you.

Ehwaz is the rune of two moving together. Its older sense is the horse and rider, but what it carries is partnership — movement that depends on more than one, and works only when each has a say in the pace. Trust here is practical, not sentimental: it is what lets you rely on another without being pulled along. Drawn for healing, it holds both sides at once — the ease of being supported, and the strain of matching someone else's speed. Which of the two it is, the rune does not say.
